utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such instances of anyone being stripped of their citizenship. I know that there were many Muslims and Bosniaks, as they were later called, who were even members of the Army of Republika Srpska. I've known some of them since my childhood, and I know that they experienced no problems with citizenship whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown P2508. What should have been added was a part from 65 ter 2382. It was the assembly in Jahorina from the 27th to 29th August and the 30th of September, 1993. You were shown page 33 in English and page 31 in the B/C/S, and we saw all sorts of things that were proposed. Were movements of population ever organised as, for example, between India and Pakistan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to document - we shan't look at it because it's not necessary - marked as 65 ter 02380 you were shown page 49 in English and page 40 in B/C/S. It was a speech of former President Karadzic about Podrinje and Gorazde and the fulfilment of the third strategic goal. Do you know whether there was any fighting in Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some clashes, but what do you mean by "fighting"? You mean at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, from Gorazde, for example? Did Gorazde go to war, because it had been declared a safe zone?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that the units from Gorazde would leave the protected zone and enter the Serbian territory, just as they did in Srebrenica. But the result of it all was that today Gorazde is administered by Bosniaks and Muslims and the number of Serbs remaining there is ridiculous. But I knew that Gorazde was a protected zone and I could hear from time to time that there were some clashes going on there and that they were the result of the phenomenon that I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: President Dodik, thank you for answering our questions. We won't take any more of your time. Thank you, and have a safe journey back unless we see each other.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, this then concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague. We're happy that you -- we can release you well in time so that you can perform your duties and return home because that is what we wish you, that is, a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask to be excused so -- to greet President Dodik, and I would have to leave the courtroom for that since he is leaving the city immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Co-counsel is there so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness apparently has arrived. Could he be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to note quickly, Mr. President, that the Court had asked yesterday about the necessity of tendering certain excerpts from the tape-recorded interview. Accordingly, I looked back at that. I think we can cut the number of exerts tendered in half. The first one was the one where the witness first initially said he wouldn't confirm anything that wasn't -- although there was a subsequent apparently confirmation and in respect of another one, I think the Court indicated to the witness when he was contextualising that the entire page would be admitted. So in light of that, I thought it best not to remove that from the list, but otherwise we'll -- we will act in accordance with the suggestion made by the Court yesterday about the need to do so in light of the witness's confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that the witness has not yet arrived at the premises?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Stojanovic, the witness apparently has not arrived. He was scheduled to arrive not later than 1.00. I suggest that we take the break now, another 20 minutes, and then have a slightly extended last session which goes until quarter past 2.00. That would be a session of one hour and 20 minutes then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's how we will proceed. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic, I do understand that the 92 ter material now does not anymore include the procedural matters some ten pages of the whole of it. Final question: The 92 -- the 65 ter summary refers to the Markale market, 28th of August, 1995, but that seems to be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake, yeah. It's the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what sounds more logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Moroz. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. As far as I understand, Serbian interpreter works here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we check -- could you check --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So for me it's better to communicate in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah ... mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness -- could the earphones be on channel 4, the English. It is. Mr. Moroz, before you give evidence and I think that's -- was part of previous experience as well. We'll keep a close eye on whether your mastering of the English language is such that we would allow you to continue in English or not, or whether we would urge you to use your native language. But we'll start as you suggest. Would you please make the solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Moroz. Mr. Moroz, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel, sir. I would first ask that you state your name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I am Sergii Moroz. Well, this is my full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I can ask you: Have you previously testified at this Tribunal in other cases?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yes, I testified previously two times, in Karadzic and -- just ... Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Galic.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Galic case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at this time I would ask for 1D03955 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that will be a transcript from the Galic case dated the 22nd and 23rd of January, 2003. Do those dates -- are they in accord with your recollection of when you testified in the Galic case? Does that sound right that you testified in January of 2003 in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, yes, but this is about Russian channels something. What does it ... what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the witness the English channel on his screen? Could we check that. Yes, we have ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is English, but this transcript is about some conversation between Judge and interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but all together it's 84 pages --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so it's not only this one page. Perhaps, Mr. Ivetic, you ask him whether he has reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have occasion to review this transcript first in the Karadzic case and then last night to see if everything is correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yes, I have a chance to look -- to look it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can briefly turn to page 3 in the e-court which will be transcript page 18116 of the underlying Galic transcript and if we could zoom in on lines 3 through 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, here your answer is recorded as saying: "I graduated from the military institute."

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "I am professional military retired lieutenant-colonel. So now I live in Kiev. I am conflict administrator in Procter & Gamble Ukraine." Is this part of the transcript still correct? That is to say, are you still employed by Procter & Gamble in that position?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: No. Currently I work in another company Unipharm Incorporated, it's American company, European small division. So I am administrative manager over there, but all the rest remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So apart from this one correction, do you stand behind the rest of the transcript as being correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if were to ask you the same questions as in the transcript today, would your answers be the same as in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, of course, when I look through yesterday the transcript, I understood that I forgot a lot of things. But now I refresh my memory and I'm absolutely sure that those days I talked the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we would then - based upon that answer - tender 1D03955 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 1D03955 receives number D1370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I have a short summary of D1370 which I have prepared and which I explained yesterday to the witness is for purposes of the public to hear what is contained therein, and I have distributed I hope to the booths in the last break. Colonel Sergii Moroz is a retired professional military lieutenant-colonel from Kiev, Ukraine, who was a member of the UNPROFOR forces in Sector Sarajevo between October 1993 through October 1994. He was a mission commander within an engineer section. His unit was a specific unit within the Sector Sarajevo headquarters whose main task was renovation and repair of civilian objects, such as electricity lines, sewage systems, water and gas systems of both warring sides. In performing the repair work, mixed working teams were formed consisting of members of the warring sides, who accompanied the UN engineers. Co-operation was very productive. Repair missions were almost every day. In relation to the electrical utilities, the repairs were mostly required to be done to pylons on Serbian-held territory. The damage was caused by gun-fire on the one hand, and by mortar fire from the Serbian side -- from the, pardon, Muslim side on the other hand. In relation to water supplies, drinking water was always available in Sarajevo. The only difficulties were due to low water pressure, such that civilians had to take water in a reservoir from the ground floor up to their apartments on higher floors. As to the gas supply, due in part to Russia cutting or diminishing the gas supply, and second that is correct gas pipelines were damaged in places. As to the supply of water, nearly all the valves to wells were on the Muslim side in Sarajevo. When the UN received complaints of the Muslim side that the Serbs had cut off the water, upon inspection, it was revealed the valves on the territory controlled by the Muslim army were, in fact, closed. During his deployment, the witness nearly every other day during the evening experienced that the Muslim side would fire mortars from near the PTT building where he was situated and the Serb side would respond. Ukrainian soldiers of UNPROFOR at the Tito barracks complained to him that it was hard to sleep because the Muslim side often did the same near that location. It was the opinion of the witness that such Muslim mortars had no military purpose. At the beginning the uniforms and weapons of the Muslim side were obsolete but near the end of the witness's deployment, he saw new uniforms and new weapons in their possession. As to the Markale explosion in 1994, a Russian UNMO involved in the investigation told the witness that the investigation revealed that the shell could not have come from the Serb side and that the explosion was too great to have been one mortar shell. The Russian officer was of the opinion that a special explosion device was brought into the market-place. Another Russian who was a member of UNPROFOR told the witness the Russian Battalion had seen, via night-vision goggles, that the Muslim soldiers would go into the neutral zone and further onto the zone of the Serb side and the next day fire would come from that same area into the city. And that concludes the summary. And I would have some additional questions for the witness, but with the assistance of the usher we can perhaps provide him with a hard copy, which might be easier to read, of the transcript than the version on the screen. And while we give time for that to happen, I can ask to turn to page 11 of the transcript in e-court. Page 11 should correspond to transcript page 18124 of the Galic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus on lines 1 through 8, sir. Here you were asked the question as follows: "Q. Mr. Moroz, can you tell us whether when going out for repair work whether did you form some mentioned working teams. Was there any need for that?" And your answer is recorded as: "A. Yes, there were such cases when mixed teams were formulated and usually it was done for two reasons. Sometimes one of the warring sides provided repair parts, and they want -- they wanted to be sure that these repair parts are really installed in the object. It was one of the reasons." Sir, can you tell us in relation to these mixed working team as what was the attitude of both the Serb and Muslim sides toward these mixed teams?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, worker who participated in those teams understood the importance for both sides of the job they did, and so they do it like normal important job.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were there any problems encountered in the work of those mixed teams?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: As far as professional point of view, no problems occurred because those people usually knew each other for long time, before war they worked together. But as for their personal relationship during the -- the job, they tried to be very polite and very conservative in relations because it was my personal opinion that they didn't want to be accused of their friends that they keep relationship with the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to page 14 in e-court and that would be transcript page 18127 of the Galic transcript, and I'd like to look at lines 18 through the end of the page and it says here -- the question you were asked is as follows: "Q. And did you know what caused the damage of these cables in Vogosca which then had such an effect that you indicated, that is, power cuts?" And you answered as follows: "A. So sometimes it was gun-fire and so the damage was not very big. Just one of the wires was cut. And the other reason was mortar fire from the Muslim side in the direction of Volkswagen plant because, as far as I know, so I'm sure of that because Muslim workers often told me that there were rumours inside the city that on that plant an ammunition work-shop was organised. I've been to that plant during the mission, and I" - and we need to turn the page - "hadn't seen any working activity on that plant, because it was seriously damaged." If I can first focus on this reference to the Volkswagen plant, can you -- can you explain for us where that plant is located in reference to the power plant?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: So it was very close to the power plant and I think that it was built there just to use the electricity from this power plant. Well, and I've seen the territory of this and I personally was inside that territory. Because my boss, French officer, asked me, just have a look on the territory, because there were rumours that some work-shop of ammunition production is organised there. Well, I asked Serbian engineers to accompany me on the territory, so they did it, and so I -- I saw that only just spare parts were obsolete, very old, are piled there, so no activity, no transport traffic so that everything was calm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the power plant that is mentioned, to which side in the conflict did that plant provide electricity, which of the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: For both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus on the part of your answer where you mentioned that wires were cut by gun-fire. Could you explain your impression of how that happened.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: So it's actually not my impression, but I -- I asked workers on both sides why wires are cut so often, what was the reason. Because when pylon is damaged by a shell, by shelling, it's visible and everything understandable. But why wires are cut. And I was told that probably fragments of -- of shells are reasons of that, and they told me that sometimes snipers so boast in front of other soldiers how so precise they are and they fired from sniper rifles shoot in the direction. Probably that, but that were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now beginning at line 12 of the same page, you were asked about problems supplying water to parts of Sarajevo. And here you mention how pumping water from reservoirs was utilised but due to lack of electricity or parts sometimes that didn't work. And if we can turn to the next page, and here at the top you say that due to the low pressure some people had to carry water up from the ground floor to their apartments, and then you say at lines 9 through 10: "Nevertheless, to drink water -- drinking water was always inside the city." And I'd like to ask you: To what part of the city did this apply, which side had drinking water available in this nature?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, there were difficulties with the water supplying because there were periods, especially during winter, when pumping stations in Ilidza, where water was pumping into the mountain of Mojmilo, were not operational due to -- sometimes the reason was lack of electricity and for some period, it was around two months, only -- there were around a dozen of engines pumping water and only several of them were operation. And that is why there was a -- it was a lack of water in reservoir in Mojmilo. Just to make water pressure enough for people to use it, in the evening, so engineer officer closed wells on the mountain of Mojmilo just to make enough stock of water in the tank on the city, and in the morning, he is -- he opened that well. Well, but even this water was not enough to make enough pressure for -- for the city, and only ground or first floor of buildings have it. I speak mostly about the old city. But there were several weeks when even on first floors water was absent, and trucks with water tanks were organised to -- well, to bring water for the population, and the main source of the water during that period was a big reservoir on the brewery, city brewery, because it was the lowest point in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we could turn to page 75 in e-court which should correlate to transcript page 18205 of the Galic transcript I would like to focus on line 17 onward where Judge El Mahdi asked you some additional questions about the water and the question was as follows: "Thank you" --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Page 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 18205 in the paper copy. And so line 17 and onwards the Judge asked you: "Thank you. Then if I may, I'd like to move on to another subject on which I need clarification. It has to do with the water supply. And I'm quoting you in English: [In English] "-- Was the section chief who examined personally pipelines. And very often he was -- he came from the mission in a bad mood because on Muslim side wells were cut off." And you answered: "Closed. Not cut off probably. I put in a wrong way. They were closed." And then General -- pardon me, Judge El Mahdi went on to say: "And who was it who did" - if we can turn the page - "that? Which side? Was it the Muslim side which closed the wells?" And you answered: "Yes." And then the Judge asked: "Why would they do that? What would they gain in this way, in your view. Was it the sabotage or what was it? " And you answered as follows: "So the greater part of valves -- I think nearly all valves were on Muslim side, and so I can't be sure about the purpose of this closure, but usually the day when it was closed UNPROFOR got complaint from Muslim side that Serbs cut off water from Sarajevo. Judge El Mahdi said then: "Yes. And it was then said -- it was claimed that it had been done in the area that was controlled by the Muslim army; is that so?" "A. Yes. Judge El Mahdi: "And how often did this happen? Was it once or more often?" And you answered: "No, no, much more than once. Dozens of times during my tour of duty, especially in the first half during winter and spring 1994." Now I'm going to ask you in relation to these circumstances, these dozen or so times, when your commander came back in a bad mood after finding that the valves to the wells were closed, do you know if it was ever officially reported within UNPROFOR that this was the case?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what were his actions -- what actions he did after such trips but usually after each mission we filled in form in computer and send it like a report or so -- the report of the day. And probably -- I'm sure he did some reports, but whether it -- what were the results and who analysed those reports, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is the "he"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you answer the Judge's question, who is the "he" that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: It was the officer -- French officer, major -- his name Philippe but I don't remember the last name because for me French last names it's very difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was he one of your supervisors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I can't say that I do remember all supervisors in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But was he one of your supervisors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Philippe, well I don't remember. More than 20 years have passed, unfortunately. But I remember that he was very frustrated about that because from the humanitarian point of view he couldn't understand why somebody did such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 22 in e-court and that will be page 18135 of the Galic transcript and it will be talking about the gas supply. And I'd like to focus beginning at line number 4 --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 18135, sir. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so beginning at line 4 the question posed was: "In what way? What information did you have concerning the gas supply to the city, and where was the city supplied with gas from?" And you answered as follows: "So I got an order from my chief to visit first gas company inside the city, and I had conversation with the chief - I do not remember his name - to clarify the reasons there were not gas in the city. So the answer was that first Russia cut -- or diminished, reduced, gas supply to Bosnia; and the second, that gas pipelines in some places were damaged and due to that, gas pressure is very low in the city. After that I went to the Serbian side and spoke to -- I mentioned this man Krajisnik. And he confirmed that information, that gas supply is reduced to a great extent and there were damages on the line but due to low pressure it is very difficult to find the places of the leak, gas leak on the lines. So only two times I've been involved in such missions and -- so no other missions I had." And the first question I want to ask is: When you say first went to a gas company inside the city, which warring party controlled that gas company?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: It was the Muslim side, and it was just distributing company, which was responsible for gas lines inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it explained to you what was meant when they said Russia cut or diminished the gas supply to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, of course, first reaction of the director was Serbs are -- are responsible for that. But after conversation why they did -- they switched off -- they cut gas, after that he explained me which you just read, the reasons you've just read. And, well, the Serbian side was responsible and controlled big pipelines which received gas from Russia, and the director of this company, transporting company, Krajisnik, explained me nearly the same which I had from the director of the first company.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the gas that was affected, which gas -- which of the warring parties was affected by these problems in the gas supply?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next, I want to move to a different topic and I want to look at page 27 in e-court, and that will be transcript page 18140 of the hard copy of the Galic transcript. And I'd like to look at lines 16 and onwards on this page, and if we're all there the question starts off asking you: "You personally during your stay, did you know about firing from mortars? And if you did, could you tell us in which situations." And your answer reads as follows: "Well, during my missions, we were not fired -- our missions were -- as far as I remember, were not fired by mortars. Usually it was just exchange -- fire exchanged between warring sides. And we were -- at that moment we were somewhere in the middle. But the greater mortar activity was during the night, and very often just close to PTT building where I was staying during the night, Muslim side -- Muslim soldiers fired from mortar and then it was an answer from Serbian side. Nearly -- especially during winter 1994, nearly each other day the night" - if we can turn the page - "started from the mortar exchange. And the same story was with Tito barracks where Ukrainian battalion was located. Officers complained to me that it's hard to sleep because very often fire exchanges [sic] took place." Now, the first question: This PTT building where you say you were located, what else was located at that building such that you would be there during the night?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Sorry, will repeat, please, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who or what was located at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: So Sector Sarajevo headquarters were -- was located over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know if anyone ever complained to the Bosnian Muslim side about their firing of mortars close to where the UN was?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was done officially, but I know that officers who contacted -- liaison officers who contacted both sides informed them about such shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus on the return fire from the Serbian side, were there complaints made by the Bosnian Muslim side about that return fire?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't know if it was done officially, but in the conversation with Serbian soldiers and officers, I heard that they complained that and asked me why UNPROFOR doesn't stop it. Well -- but all of that was unofficial conversation on my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood. And if we could turn to page 38 in the Galic transcript, which will correlate to transcript page 18151, you are again being asked about this shelling from the PTT building and this time the Judge's question beginning at line 14 is as follows: "May I interrupt you. I think that this is not exactly the information that you're seeking, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. "Do you have any personal opinion as to whether militarily it is acceptable to fire from a place which is -- was a short distance from the PTT building? And your answer was as follows: "Well, my opinion is the following: From the military point of view, there was no use firing mortar shelling from that area." And, sir, I'd like for you to explain to us militarily why -- what you meant when you said there was no use in the mortar shelling that the Bosnian Muslim side was doing from near the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, when mortar shelling is used, it -- it should be from a militarily point of view some targets should be reached. Well, some -- I don't know units, diminished, destroyed, but it should be accompanied by infantry actions, small-armour shelling, so on and so forth. It should be some co-ordinated actions. But when people did four, five round shelling and then -- so withdrew their weapons from that point and that is all, I see no reasons in that. Just only -- just only to make it public, to make it some familiar noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before you turn to another topic. Could you tell us where did those shells land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, because usually it was at night and it was somewhere in the mountains. So ... it was a very often from my point of view, because I saw only the place of shelling from the balcony where I lived. We -- I personally several times saw it and where shell was directed, it was very hard to -- to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have another question. You said shelling with mortars doesn't make any sense if there's no follow-up infantry, et cetera. Was that common that if one of the parties was shelling using mortars, that there be would a follow-up with infantry? Could you please explain that for both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several military operations, so considerable clashes, when infantry and even heavy mortar was used in some areas of Sarajevo. But usually this mortar exchange fire was very sporadic, and it seems to me it was just to exert psychological pressure on each other. Both sides used that tactics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because this Chamber has heard quite some evidence about mortars being fired and very often without any infantry activity accompanying it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you refer to as just psychological pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you give us an assessment on how much of the mortars being fired was the psychological pressure and how much of it was in support of any infantry activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to say, but I can say that more or less big infantry actions was during my year of duty in Sarajevo, probably a couple of months. All the rest it was just sporadic fire exchange, sniper activities -- snipers killed a lot of people, mostly civilians, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I asked you without referring to any one of the sides, was that the same for both sides or was there a difference in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw -- personally me, I saw mostly inside Sarajevo because I lived in PTT which was located inside Sarajevo, and so was moving around the city on APC. Also most -- the greater part of my missions were inside Sarajevo. That is why I saw more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say because of your limited movement you were -- naturally saw only part of it and that is mainly, if I understand you well, incoming fire in Muslim-held territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to page 64 in e-court of the transcript, and that will correlate to page 18186 in the paper copy of the underlying Galic transcript. And I'd like to start at line 23 of the same in relation to an answer that you are giving. And you say: "Yes. I remember now what I meant when saying that. Serbs -- the Serbian side very frequently blamed Muslim side that Muslim snipers used neutral zone or even went on Serbian territory, shoot from the Serbian" - next page - "territory at civilian citizens and even killed them just to -- just to provoke firing back and to blame Serbian side in atrocities. I couldn't -- so personally I couldn't neither prove nor disprove that. But I had a conversation with a Russian UNPROFOR officer which I met after the Russian battalion arrival in February -- it seems to me it was in February, yeah -- in February 1994. They had -- the Russian Battalion had a couple of check-points just close to the river on the -- again, on the south bank of the river. Now, I know that. Well, and this officer, lieutenant, it seems to me -- it seems to me I remember his family name Chervonenko. It is a Ukrainian family name. That is why I remember." And then you were asked to spell the name and you say at line 17 onward: "Of course not. It is misspelt. So C-h-e-r-v-o-n-e-n-k-o. Correct. And I met him during one of my missions. So I need his information how to find the spot of the water pipeline damage. And after the mission I had a conversation with him and asked about shooting activity in his area. And he told me an interesting thing. The Russian Battalion was equipped the with night vision binoculars, night vision equipment, and his soldiers and personally he himself during the night duty saw Muslim soldiers going into the neutral zone and further. And during the next day there was active shooting from that direction" - and if we just go to the top of the next page to finish up - "and he told me that such night movements of soldiers equipped with sniper rifle was regular, nearly each night. "Well, that is -- that is why I told you that I think there were reasons by Serbian side to demand that all cease-fire agreements should be signed by all warring parties." And then you were asked a follow-up question at line 18 on the same page, if we could scroll down to that, by the Judge. You were asked: "Sir, would you please clarify your answer as to were there some soldiers coming from where, crossing from what part and what part, and then subsequently the fire was observed." And your answer was: "The officer told me that soldiers went from the old city, crossed the river, and then went in the south direction up to the hill where -- which was the area of Serbian forces -- the position of Serbian forces. Well, and during the day the fire was done in the direction of the old city." Now, Colonel, in relation to what you're describing here that the Russian Battalion officer told you about, what was the belief of the Russians as understood by you of who was actually conducting this firing in the direction of the old city?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I -- my previous opinion and his words, his opinion when we discussed that in informal situation, were that both are -- both sides are shooting in both directions. And, of course, there were Serbian snipers who wanted to reach military aim; and there were Muslim snipers who shoot the same direction, just to gain probably political or some other things, just to accuse Serbian side about atrocities. But, at the same time, he told me then from Serbian side military people also went to the old city and disappeared there and it was movement -- all night was movement in both directions, and it was for 100 per cent it was very hard to say who shoot where.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we could turn to page 40 in e-court and that will be transcript page 18153 of the Galic transcript. And if we could focus on line number 23, and you were asked as follows: "Last question: Did you happen to see weapons in the city of, of whatever nature? And if yes, what did you see and where? "A. Well, usually I had close contacts with civilians inside the old" - if we could turn the page at the top - "city, because streets were narrow and it was a safe area to walk. As for the weapons, I already told you that in the first period of my tour of duty I saw that weapons was rather obsolete -- I mean on Muslim side inside the city. Sometimes it were shotguns of Second World War period. But at the time just before I left Sarajevo, I could say that at that period soldiers were dressed in new uniforms and they had new small fire." Now, first of all, could you explain for us in addition to the new uniforms you say they had new small fire. What did you mean by saying "new small fire," what kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I mean guns and automatic guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was this discussed within UNPROFOR -- was it discussed where these new uniforms and weapons were coming from?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, of course, in personal conversations with officers, for us it was very strange how blocked city can survive in blockade and more -- moreover, fight back, because for shooting and shelling you need weapons and shells and ammunition. So there were rumours - only rumours - that it was some underground tunnel. My colleagues, Ukrainian officers, who often were on duty in the airport told me that they heard that some tunnel is in the airport area. Muslim workers which I worked with told me that there was special tunnel somewhere in the old city in the area Bascarsija; I can mispronounce it, but it sounds like something like that. It was famous area in Sarajevo for criminal activity. And during the war, it was the centre of drugs, illegal weapons, so on and so forth. And civilians told that somewhere -- the tunnel is somewhere there. But, of course, I never seen myself this tunnel and cannot support those rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When asking about rumours, Mr. Ivetic, have you checked with the Prosecution whether there's any dispute about the existence of a tunnel at the airport? Because we now hear that there were rumours about that. Is it the position of the Prosecution that there was or there wasn't or do you have no position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We believe there was indeed a tunnel there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The tunnel at the airport there was. We're heard now about a different tunnel and we had three witnesses of the Prosecution that denied the tunnel in the airport --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, no, I want to -- Mr. Ivetic, if would you have focussed your questions on another tunnel, I would not have intervened. My question is: We now hear of rumours of a tunnel of which apparently both parties agree that -- unless you disagree that it existed at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot lead -- ask leading questions, so I have to ask open-ended questions and then use the answers from the witness to elicit information about this secretary tunnel that we did not have previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't mind if would you take off your hand from your mouth when you're speaking. But I think you can -- you could have introduced the matter of another tunnel by putting to the witness what is apparently not in dispute, such as it's not in dispute between the parties that there was a tunnel at the airport. Is that the only tunnel you are aware of on a the basis of his early testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if we could follow up. You indicated the old city and then you tried to pronounce it. Is the area that you referring to located near Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah, probably you pronounce it better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And apart from the rumours as the two tunnels, was there any other discussion amongst yourself at UNPROFOR as to any potential source for the new weapons and uniforms that the Muslim side had at the end of your tour?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, there also some people -- for instance, Serbians were absolutely sure, Serbian side was absolutely sure the UN convoys were used for that. And there was -- they supposed that it somehow -- some trucks which were added to UN convoys and were -- and so drove inside the city. Well, I don't know if it is true or not, but there was one rather big scandal when Serbian side shoot at UNHCR convoy and several trucks disappeared. And Serbs told that they took away weapons with their trucks. But what was -- again, it was like rumours or -- I haven't seen any official documents regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one other topic that you were asked about during the Galic trial was the topic of the Markale shelling in 1994, and that is discussed at several places in the transcript. I'd like to go to page 32 in the transcript which is page 18145 of the transcript, and I want to talk about your own observations after going to the scene of the market after the explosion. And on this page it will start with line 6 and go to 16. And here you say: "Well, it will be a little bit long answer. First I have had -- I've seen the results of the explosion on TV, so nearly 20 or 30 minutes after the explosion all that was life report on local TV. Well, the next day I had mission not far from the market-place, and I visited that and just saw -- examined the place of the explosion. And for me -- so on TV it was told that it was a mortar shell. After I've seen what I saw, the market-place, for me it was very strange that it was -- the cause of the explosion was identified as mortar shell because it was inside the city and buildings are rather high, and so to my mind trajectory of the shell -- so that the place of the explosion couldn't be at the place it was." Now, in relation to your personal observations, what did you mean by saying it was very strange the place of the explosion couldn't be at the place it was?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, after a rather -- after some time of working inside the old city, you understand, with the help of civilians who live there, what side of the city is safe, what is unsafe, and usually if you -- during my first mission, when I went by foot on unsafe side, people always told me, So come out of there because better work here, not there, and the main reason was mortar shelling. And I should say that the place of -- where traces of this explosion were couldn't be so close to buildings because they were rather high and the trajectory of shell couldn't be so close to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to your trip to the Markale market-place, how did you know the exact place of the explosion? Did someone tell you where to look?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, this market-place is not so big, first of all. Then on TV, everything was shown in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then at several times in the Galic transcript you talk about a Russian in the UNMO mission to hold you the mortar shell could not have come from the Serb side. I want to turn to page 45 in e-court, transcript page 18167 of the Galic transcript, and here you are talking about what this Russian told you and from line 1 it reads as follows. The question is: "Sir, could you repeat what you said. Did he tell you that the mortar could not have come from the Serb side or --" And your answer: "Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Judging from the possible trajectory is the first reason. The second reason, that the direction of fragments left after the explosion on asphalt showed it couldn't be from the Serbian side. And the second -- the might -- a number of fragments of the explosion was so huge that any -- and a number of victims was very big. It couldn't have be done by mortar shell, by mortar round? "Q. So what you're saying is he told you that it could not have been a mortar shell or that the shell could not have originated from the Serb side? Which of it? "A. Both. Both. It can be -- if it were a shell -- a mortar shell, it couldn't come from Serbian side. But the character of the explosion shows that the explosion was bigger than any mortar -- any mortar. "Q. Did he tell you what it would have been? "A. No. His supposition was that a special explosion device was brought into the market-place." And, sir, my first question: How did you understand and what did you mean when you said that the number of victims was very big, it couldn't be done by a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, statistics show that in results of mortar shelling, usually by one round, only several -- several person can be killed. For me, when I arrived in Sarajevo and saw on asphalt traces of mortar explosions was very strange that they were insignificant. And then I was explained that usually -- both sides used not big mortars which were -- which can be moved by hand. That is why they were -- their might was not so big. And traces were just not very deep inside asphalt or probably asphalt was of a very good quality. But in the market, the trace was much deeper and it was -- the fragments which were traces of fragments which were on asphalt were dispersed evenly in all directions. And usually when trajectory -- when mortar shell was coming and after explosion, it was some angle of these fragments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, part of the testimony we hear now is hearsay from another person who apparently gives expert opinion, although we do not know whether he qualifies as an expert, and we now are asking this witness to interpret the words of that unknown person that may or may not qualify as an expert, we do not know, because we don't know who it is. Now similarly, in addition to that, you are eliciting evidence at this moment from the witness which apparently is something for which we heard a lot of experts, and that's not what really assists the Chamber greatly in finding the truth on these matters. You may proceed and please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. But I think that what the -- part of the witness has been telling us is based on his own observations from the scene, and I can ask him if that's accurate. But that's how I understood the portion of his answer to be related to his personal observations from viewing the site. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's part of -- I started with the first part, which I said was not assisting. The second part still requires -- of course, he observed a few things, but he also drew a lot of conclusions about that and that means that he makes it opinion evidence, expert evidence, where his qualifications as an expert are not established. So you have responded to part of my observation, and that part also still stands as to the extent it assists this Chamber. Please keep this in mind when you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you are still on this page, maybe I could just ask some question for clarification. Sir, you said -- this is page 18167 that the -- "so his supposition was that a special explosion device was brought into the market-place. What kind of special explosion device could this be that could be brought into the market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say, because I am sure -- you see, I visited the market-place several times after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sure. Okay. You don't know. Sorry. You don't know what kind. Now if it is brought on to the market-place, would it be able to make such a deep crater as you said it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Deeper traces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not traces. Crater.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crater, okay. Was deeper because probably the explosion was bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But you've got to know the explosion -- you don't know the explosion, he didn't know the explosion because you both [Overlapping speakers] ... that's a -- that's guess-work now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when you see a big cave, you understand that explosion was bigger than [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's very true. But if you did see a big cave like -- it more explains that this thing came at force rather than being put there and making a hole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Because I can compare what I have seen in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you. You don't agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you said when you see a big cave. Can you describe how big that cave was. How deep it was, what its dimensions were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually after traces on asphalt after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- normal and widely seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no, no, I'm stopping you here. You said, When you see a big cave. Did you see a big cave on the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you describe the dimensions of that cave; that is, length, width and depth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it was -- diameter was around 30 centimetres and the depth was 5, 7 centimetres. As far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you -- as -- as -- as to compare to hundreds of traces which were around the city, there were usually 2, 3 centimetres depth and the round was 10, 15 centimetres and then all the rest, traces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you drew your conclusions on the basis that the diameter was 30 centimetres rather than 10 to 15, and then the depth was 5 to 7 centimetres compared to 2 or 3 centimetres you observed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any special training in interpreting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this Russian officer you spoke with -- and at transcript page 18155 of the Galic case, you say it's Mr. Rumyantsev. Where were you both when you talked about this Markale shelling?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: We were in informal -- somewhere at night, informal situation in PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're about -- looks like a minute or half a minute past -- before the break. I have approximately three more questions so I don't know if we should continue or if we should end for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had already an extended session because we started a bit earlier. I think for tomorrow we don't need the whole of tomorrow's time anyhow and the next witness would be available only on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think the next witness is available tomorrow and Thursday via videolink. That was my understanding. But we could check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- then I may be -- for both days he would be available on -- One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, if those who are assisting us have no problems with it, then the Chamber would prefer that you, with three questions, conclude your examination-in-chief. And, of course, it also depends on whether Mr. Mladic, because we'll easily move to tomorrow if that is preferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I saw my client nodding and so I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw a similar thing, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the Galic -- pardon me. At the time that you discussed this with Mr. Rumyantsev, did you have any access to any official reports of the incident?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the Galic transcript, you were -- and the Karadzic case, you were asked about a Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolay Vasilievich Rumyantsev, and that was at transcript page 18170 through -72 of the Galic transcript and at 29539 and 29541 of the Karadzic transcript. And in the Galic case, you talked about an Aleksei Rumyantsev. Do you know if the Russian officer whom you spoke with and whom you remembered to be Aleksei Rumyantsev is the same or different than Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolay Vasilievich Rumyantsev that you were asked about in these prior cases?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Probably I named him -- his first name in wrong way because I knew -- I studied at the military institute with another guy Rumyantsev, and that is why I remember clearly the name of this UNMO officer, because he also studied at the same military institute but a little bit later than me. And probably I just mixed up their names and that is why I named him Aleksei Rumyantsev. But I never knew his second -- father name, Vasilievich, that is why ... but I am sure that I am speaking at the officer, UNMO Russian officer, then he was major not lieutenant-colonel. In Sarajevo, he was a major, well, and his name was Rumyantsev.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now has -- the Prosecution has examined you in both the Galic and the Karadzic cases. Has anything caused you to change or doubt your memory of what the Russian officer named Rumyantsev whom you spoke with about the Markale market explosion?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure that everything I told during those two cases is the truth. And after my first visit of the market-place and we exchanged views on what was happened -- what had happened in the market with Rumyantsev, I visited on -- with missions the market area several times, and several times I came to the place, and after our discussion and when he pin-point some things, peculiar things which I should pay attention to, I paid, and that is why I am absolutely sure what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you again for your patience and for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm completed with direct, and then I await Your Honours' preferences as to with -- with which witness we start with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. But perhaps -- no, I -- I have to ask you to still wait for us because thinking about scheduling. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, if there's a question about moving what had been fixed as the commencement of the videolink for tomorrow, it also implicates the scheduling for the Prosecution - specifically in this case me and my availability on Thursday - so I had anticipated, as discussed, that we would be beginning on -- tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was some confusion about -- amongst ourselves about the availability of the videolink. I do understand that the next witness would be ready tomorrow to start at 9.30 his videolink evidence. The Chamber would like to start tomorrow mourning with that videolink evidence. Mr. Ivetic, could you remind me about the times needed so that we can give a better instruction to the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the time estimates are one and a half on the Defence and two and a half on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One and a half and two and a half makes up four hours. Perhaps some additional questions. Could the Prosecution tell us how much time -- I think it was one hour and a half for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which would mean anyhow that we would have a session on Thursday because we'll not finish the videolink evidence tomorrow and the present witness. Now since we need a session on Thursday anyhow, I think it would be best to start cross-examination on Thursday morning and ask this witness to be available on Thursday morning. If that is agreeable to all parties, Witness, tomorrow we will not start with your cross-examination. That will be only on Thursday. Therefore, we'd like to see you back Thursday, 9.30 in the morning most likely, it can be that you have to wait for a second, but 9.30 in the morning for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, just so we're clear. Assuming that we don't complete the videolink tomorrow, although I know the parties will be attempting to do so, I presume we would continue with the videolink on Thursday morning until completed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we hope that we will be able to complete it tomorrow. Witness, we'd like to see you back on Thursday morning, 9.30 in the morning, and we hope to start right away; but if not, I beg for some patience. I further instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given or testimony still to be given on Thursday. If that's clear, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 9th of December, 9.30 in the morning, this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of December, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
